issue.title: Money lessons in school, and a rebalanced GCSE maths: who decides what goes in?
issue.question: Should schools teach money skills like inflation, savings and mortgages, even if it means less of other maths, and who decides what is dropped?
issue.summary: On 22 November 2026 the Department for Education announced changes to the curriculum to teach pupils how to manage money. Primary pupils will learn to judge whether a deal is good value, and secondary pupils will learn why prices rise, how savings grow, how to spot scams and how mortgages work (s1). Maths will remove unnecessary content, and GCSE maths will be rebalanced, especially at foundation tier, towards financial maths and statistics, but the announcement does not say what will be cut, gives no start date and does not mention a consultation (s1). The department says further details will come "in the coming weeks" (s1).
issue.slot_reason: Schools last came up in the simulation on 9 November, and on 22 November the government announced new money lessons and a rebalanced GCSE maths, which was in the UK news today. It asks who decides what children learn when something has to give way.

news.headline: Government announces financial literacy push in national curriculum reforms

poll.finding: 89% of parents think financial education should be taught in schools. The page does not give the question wording and does not ask what should be dropped to make room, so it is not the same question as this one.

Reading, writing and real-world money: nine in ten parents demand a new 'fourth R'

tests.text: Children leave school knowing mortgages, savings and scams.
Small trials in a few schools show maths holds up before every school changes.
Teachers and parents help choose what goes, not ministers alone.
Maths hours and basics don't shrink to make room for money lessons.
Teachers aren't handed extra work without extra time or pay.
Nothing gets cut without a trial or parents being told.

voices.who: 42, South West, in work, social renter
voices.text: Yes! My kids got tricked on loans. Teach them. Just don’t make it a box to tick.

voices.who: 78, South West, in work, social renter
voices.text: Yes, and teach how bills and climate connect. Don’t make it a sales pitch for banks.

voices.who: 37, South East, in work, owns outright
voices.text: Teach them how not to get ripped off. Don’t let it replace proper maths.

voices.who: 77, South East, retired, owns with a mortgage
voices.text: Separate lessons. Maths should stay maths. Don’t cut the proper maths we all learned.

voices.who: 75, South West, in work, private renter
voices.text: Keep the maths. Teach money at home, not school. Don’t leave kids with less maths.

voices.who: 56, East of England, in work, owns outright
voices.text: Don’t know enough. Ask the teachers. Don’t let it be decided in Westminster alone.

bench.title: Money lessons trial: maths hours kept, 40 schools drawn by lot
bench.answer: The Education Secretary may not cut any GCSE maths content or hours in a school until the Department for Education has run this trial and published the result. Trial: 40 state secondary schools, drawn by lot from willing schools in one region, teach the money lessons inside the same maths hours. They are compared with 40 similar schools that change nothing and lose nothing. Teachers and parents help pick what content moves, and schools get paid cover time. Provisional fail number: if foundation-tier maths results fall more than 2 points against the comparison schools, stop. Stop date: 31 August 2028. Primary schools and sixth forms are left out. Pass: if results hold, it may extend, and must tell parents first.

bench.title: Teachers and parents pick what maths drops, tested in 40 schools
bench.answer: The Education Secretary must not cut any GCSE maths content until a panel has approved it. The panel would have a majority of serving maths teachers and parent governors, with ministers holding no vote. In 40 schools drawn by lot, the panel chooses what money content replaces, with no cut to maths hours. Another 40 drawn schools keep today's course. Both are marked on the same maths paper. Fail: if trial pupils score more than 3 percentage points lower (provisional), the trial stops and nothing is cut. Stop date: 31 August 2028. Parents are told in writing. It leaves out schools outside the draw and pupils already past Year 9. Pass: the panel publishes results, then may widen the trial.

bench.title: Let school communities own the money lessons
bench.answer: A mortgage lesson should teach children to question the deal, not admire the bank. Let elected school panels of teachers, parents and pupils commission shared, advert-free lessons on savings, mortgages and scams. Teachers replace textbook exercises, not maths topics; panels publish every swap. Keep maths hours. Education ministers fund preparation time and independent marking. Draw lots among 30 volunteer schools: half try it, half continue unchanged. After one year, require a provisional ten-percentage-point gain in money skills with no fall in maths against the other schools. Publish separate results for disadvantaged pupils and pupils with special educational needs. Stop after that year unless Parliament renews it on those results; passing earns wider rollout.
